target_year_over_year_context.explanation: This is a many-to-many split. D156 (2023) covers the AMLA broadly: reforming/modernizing BSA, risk-based approach, Treasury priorities, enforcement expansion, whistleblower protections, and FinCEN priorities. In 2024, this broad AMLA topic is split into multiple disclosures: D150 covers the consolidated BSA/AMLA framework; D151 covers the AMLA impact depending on rulemaking and FinCEN priorities; D152 covers the Corporate Transparency Act (enacted as part of AMLA); D153 covers specific proposed/adopted rules for investment advisers under AMLA/BSA. Each 2024 disclosure addresses a specific sub-topic introduced or contained within D156. We provide separate rows for the logical links: D156->D151 (AMLA impact/priorities), D156->D152 (AMLA/CTA), D156->D153 (AMLA/Investment Adviser rules), and D156->D150 (AMLA/BSA framework). Note: D150 is also linked from D155. This is allowed as separate rows.

current_disclosures.summary: The impact of the AMLA depends on additional rulemakings and implementation guidance, though the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has already issued required anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism priorities. These priorities include corruption, cybercrime, terrorist financing, fraud, transnational crime, drug trafficking, human trafficking, and proliferation financing.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: The Corporate Transparency Act (CTA), enacted in 2021 as part of the AMLA, established beneficial ownership information reporting requirements implemented by a FinCEN rule effective in 2024. Domestic companies formed before 2024 must file initial reports by January 1, 2025 (later announced as March 21, 2025), while those formed in or after 2024 must file within 90 or 30 days of formation, subject to exemptions.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Anti-Money Laundering and Anti-Bribery Rules and Regulations
current_disclosures.summary: In 2024, FinCEN and the SEC proposed rules requiring investment advisers to implement procedures to identify and verify customer identities, and FinCEN proposed amendments to BSA program requirements including periodic risk assessments. Additionally, FinCEN adopted a rule effective January 1, 2026, including certain investment advisers in the definition of 'financial institutions' under BSA rules, prescribing minimum AML/CFT program standards and suspicious activity reporting obligations.

comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC explicitly identify the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) as the foundational legal framework for anti-money laundering and financial transparency. Both disclosures cite similar core obligations under the BSA, including customer verification, transaction monitoring, and reporting suspicious activities to detect money laundering and terrorism financing. While GS focuses heavily on the recent comprehensive reform of these laws via the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), BAC notes the same BSA requirements and additionally mentions 2024 proposed regulatory amendments to update AML program requirements for supervised institutions.

sentences.text: The U.S. Bank Secrecy Act, as amended (BSA), including by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), contains anti-money laundering and financial transparency laws and authorizes or mandates the promulgation of various regulations applicable to financial institutions, including standards for verifying client identification at account opening, and obligations to monitor client transactions and report suspicious activities.
Through these and other provisions, the BSA seeks, among other things, to promote the identification of parties that may be involved in terrorism, money laundering or other suspicious activities.

For example, we are subject to the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), which contains anti-money laundering and financial transparency laws designed to detect and deter money laundering and the financing of terrorism, as well as record-keeping, reporting, due diligence and customer verification requirements, various sanctions programs administered and enforced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and foreign jurisdictions, which target entities or individuals that are, or are located in countries that are, involved in activities, such as terrorism, hostilities, drug trafficking or human rights violations and the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and the U.K. Bribery Act, relating to corrupt and illegal payments to government officials and others.

comparisons.comparison: Both GS and JPM disclose the U.S. Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) as a key anti-money laundering regulation. Both specifically highlight the requirement for financial institutions to establish 'risk-based' systems or approaches to internal controls to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing. JPM explicitly states this requirement in the context of the BSA, while GS details this risk-based approach as a codification under the newer Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), which reformed the BSA.

sentences.text: Among other things, the AMLA codifies a risk-based approach to anti-money laundering compliance for financial institutions; requires the U.S. Department of the Treasury to periodically promulgate priorities for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism; requires the development of standards by the U.S. Department of the Treasury for testing technology and internal processes for BSA compliance; expands enforcement- and investigation-related authority, including a significant expansion in the available sanctions for certain BSA violations; and expands BSA whistleblower incentives and protections.

The Bank Secrecy Act ("BSA") requires all financial institutions, including banks and securities broker-dealers, to establish a risk-based system of internal controls reasonably designed to prevent money laundering and the financing of terrorism.

In the U.S., the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001 and the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020, imposes significant obligations on financial institutions to detect and deter money laundering and terrorist financing activity, including requiring banks, broker-dealers, futures commission merchants, introducing brokers and mutual funds to develop and implement AML programs, verify the identity of customers that maintain accounts, and monitor and report suspicious activity to appropriate law enforcement or regulatory authorities.
